implemented_requirements.evidence: game.py → handle_keydown() maps arrow/WASD keys to direction constants (UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT) and calls snake.change_direction(); snake.py → change_direction() queues the new direction.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Randomly placed food items on the board
implemented_requirements.evidence: food.py → Food.randomize_position() builds a list of free cells (excluding snake.body) and selects one with random.choice.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Snake grows in length after eating food
implemented_requirements.evidence: game.py → step() detects snake.head == food position, increments score and does `self.snake.grow_pending += 1`; snake.py → update() uses grow_pending to keep the tail instead of popping it, thus growing the snake.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Game ends on collision with self
implemented_requirements.evidence: snake.py → update() checks `if new_head in body_to_check: return False` (self‑collision). Game.step() ends the game when update() returns False.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Game ends on collision with boundary
implemented_requirements.evidence: snake.py → update() verifies `0 <= new_head[0] < GRID_WIDTH` and `0 <= new_head[1] < GRID_HEIGHT`; returns False on wall collision, causing Game.end_game().
game.py → run() accumulates `move_timer` and calls `self.step()` at intervals; render() redraws grid, food, snake each frame.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Current score displayed based on food eaten
implemented_requirements.evidence: game.py → render() calls `draw_text(..., f"Score: {self.score}", ...)` after each move; score is increased in step() when food is eaten.

settings.py defines DIFFICULTY_LEVELS (Easy, Medium, Hard, Insane); game.py → menu allows LEFT/RIGHT to cycle difficulty, and move_interval is set from the selected level’s speed; score multiplier is taken from the level.

judge.summary: The provided source files implement a complete, classic Snake game. Directional controls, random food placement, growth mechanics, collision detection (self and walls), per‑move board refresh, score display, and a selectable set of difficulty levels are all present and wired together. The code appears ready to run with pygame, so the submission meets all core requirements.
